items.title: Buddhist activist moves Supreme Court against singing full version of Vande Mataram; terms it Islamophobic
items.summary: A petition has been filed before the Supreme Court challenging two Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) orders that mandate the singing of all six stanzas of national song Vande Mataram at formal State events [ BD Borkar v. Union of India ]. The petition has been moved by BD Borkar, a Nagpur-based Buddhist activist, Ambedkarite scholar and civil rights advocate. Drawing on anti-caste traditions, Borkar has contended that the MHA orders dated January 28, 2026, and July 9, 2026, illegally replace the 79-year-old practice of singing a standalone, non-theistic two-stanza poem with the full version containing explicit anti-Muslim invective. "Under the guise of providing directions on the playing and singing of an ‘official version’... the impugned orders repealed the existing National Song... and imposed a new National Song which is the six-stanza civil war song of Anandamath with its unconstitutional idolatrous and Islamophobic content," the plea states. As per the plea, for nearly eight decades since Independence, India peaceably adopted a standalone two-stanza version of Vande Mataram . Written in the early 1870s, this version pre-dates the novel Anandamath written by Bankim Chandra Chatte

A Division Bench of Justice NS Sanjay Gowda and Justice JL Odedra also noted that one of the 'benami' mobile phones used by the judicial officer was acquired from a practicing advocate, with whom he exchanged as many as 186 phonecalls between June 2007 and May 2008. The Court termed this improper conduct on the judicial officer's part. "A Judicial Officer should not associate himself with practicing advocates and has to maintain a distance from the advocates to prevent any impression of impropriety.
